title: Preface
text:
How this book works
This book is for public health practitioners who already know how to do the work — the epidemiology, the surveillance, the briefings — but are being asked to do it in R. Maybe your agency is moving off SAS. Maybe a collaborator handed you a .R file and you want to understand it. Maybe you’ve opened RStudio, stared at a blank script, and closed it again.
This book is not a general introduction to R. It is not a statistics textbook. It will not teach you epidemiology. It assumes you already have domain knowledge and gives you the R fluency to apply it.
This book has one job: get a practicing epidemiologist writing, running, and sharing R-based analyses as fast as possible.
Every chapter builds on one analysis: a COVID-19 briefing for a state health commissioner. You start with a raw CSV and a blank folder. By the end, you have a self-updating report that pulls live data and publishes itself. Each chapter introduces exactly one new skill and shows you why it earns its place in the workflow — not as an exercise, but as a real improvement to something you built yourself in the chapter before.
Work through the chapters in order. They are designed to be read with R open in front of you, running the code as you go.

text:
What you need to bring

R and Quarto installed on your machine
RStudio or Positron as your editor
A folder where you keep projects
Epidemiological concepts you already know — rates, counts, surveillance cadence

You do not need prior programming experience. You do not need to clone this repository. Everything you need to run is in the book itself.

title: 1  Modern R and Public Health
text:
1.1 Why R
Public health work is converging on R. This chapter gets your workspace ready so chapter 1 can start with code.
If your agency runs SAS, you already know the core loop: read data in, reshape it, summarize it, output it. R does the same thing. The difference is everything around that loop.
Free. No license. No seat-count negotiation with procurement. No renewal cycle. R runs on a laptop, a server, or a cloud VM — same tool, same code.
Analysis lives in a script. Every step is recorded. Six months later you run the same file and get the same answer. When the Commissioner asks “where did this number come from,” you show the code.
Reports update themselves. Quarto — the tool this book is built with — embeds code directly in a document. Change a number upstream and the table in the PDF changes with it. No more copy-pasting from Excel into Word.
The public health ecosystem is here. CDC, state health departments, and academic epi groups publish R code. Reading it — and writing it — is a basic competency the field is converging on.
The tidyverse maps to what you already know. SAS DATA steps and PROC steps have direct equivalents:
Syntax changes. Mental model mostly doesn’t.

1.2 How this works
Every chapter builds on one analysis: a COVID-19 briefing for a Connecticut health commissioner. You start with a raw CSV and an empty folder. Chapter by chapter the analysis gains new capabilities — until at the end you have a self-updating report that anyone on your team could run.
Each chapter introduces exactly one new skill. The skill earns its place by solving a real problem in the analysis — not as an exercise, but as a genuine improvement to what you built before.
Code along. Every code block in this book is meant to be run, not just read. Open R before you start each chapter and keep it open.
One thing to know about R before you start: unlike SAS, R is interactive. When you run code, results appear immediately in your session. Objects — datasets, plots, numbers — live in memory and you can inspect them at any time. Think of it less like submitting a batch job and more like a conversation with your data.

title: 1  Modern R and Public Health
text:
1.7 The scenario
It’s spring of 2020 and you are working as an analyst for the Connecticut Department of Public Health’s Pandemic Incident Command. You are tasked with preparing a briefing for the Commissioner so that they can in turn brief the governor on the current situation.
The first standing question is this: Is it getting worse in Hartford, or not?
Today we are going to answer that question, click by click. Slowly we will build up our R knowledge and reduce friction until we have an analysis we can share with others.

1.7.1 Folder Structure
It is good practice to stick with a common folder layout for each of your projects. Different programming languages have different conventions but many layouts are very similar. This reduces the cognitive load for yourself and others when navigating larger projects. There are tools for creating, saving, and sharing project templates, but for now we will do this by hand.

Create a new folder called covid-briefing wherever you keep projects.
Inside it, create these folders one at a time:

data
R
scripts
outputs
docs

Inside data, create two more folders: raw and processed.
Inside outputs, create two more folders: figures and tables.

At the end you should have a folder structure that looks like this:
covid-briefing/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv   ← you'll add this shortly
│   └── processed/
├── R/
├── scripts/
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── docs/
Why these specific folders?








Folder
Purpose
Rule




data/raw
Exactly what you downloaded
Never edit a file in here.


data/processed
Cleaned data you can trust
Always regenerable from raw + a script


R
Reusable functions
Empty today — used once you stop copy-pasting


scripts
Numbered analysis steps
01_, 02_, … so the order is obvious


outputs/figures
Plots
Never hand-edited; always regenerated


outputs/tables
Summary CSVs etc…
Same rule as figures


docs
Reports
Empty today — used when you build the briefing doc





1.7.2 Open the Project in Your IDE
Once the folders exist, open the project in RStudio or Positron so that every path you write in code is relative to covid-briefing/, not to your Desktop or Downloads folder.
RStudio: File → New Project → Existing Directory → select covid-briefing → Create Project.
Positron: File → Open Folder → select covid-briefing.
Either way, the IDE will reopen with covid-briefing as your working directory. This matters throughout the rest of the book.


1.7.3 Getting the Data

Go to the dataset page: https://data.ct.gov/Health-and-Human-Services/COVID-19-Tests-Cases-and-Deaths-By-Town-ARCHIVE/28fr-iqnx
Click Export → CSV to download it.
Move the downloaded file into data/raw/.
Rename it to include the date you downloaded it, e.g.: ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv

The date stamp matters more than it looks like it should. This dataset is revised after the fact — Connecticut DPH updates prior dates as new reports come in. Stamping the filename is how you’ll later be able to say “this analysis used the data as it existed on this date,” which is exactly the kind of question a Commissioner will ask you.
From this point forward: never open this file and edit it by hand. If something about it needs to change, that change happens in a script, not in the file itself.






Note



Want to check your folder structure against a reference? See project-snapshots/after-ch-00 on GitHub for what covid-briefing/ should look like at this point.




1.7.4 Diving In
Workspace is ready, data is in data/raw/. Next chapter: write your first R code.

title: 2  Loading Your First Dataset
text:
2.1 Packages
Your workspace is set up and your raw data is sitting in data/raw/. Time to write your first R code.
R ships with a base set of tools. On top of that, the community has built thousands of packages — collections of ready-made code you can install and use without writing everything yourself. These are distributed through CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), R’s official package repository.
The family of packages we’ll lean on most is called the tidyverse — a curated set of tools that share a common design and work well together. We’ll introduce them one at a time. This chapter uses three of them plus a few helpers for reading, writing, and navigating files.

  "here" # for building paths that work everywhere

title: 2  Loading Your First Dataset
text:
2.2 Reading Data Files

2.2.1 Reading our Comma Delimited File (.csv)
We are going to do a few things here:

Load the packages we need into our session.
Build a path to our data file and save it as csv_path.
Read the data into our session and save it as covid_data.


library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(fs)
library(here)



2.2.2 Paths and here()
Before reading the file, a word on paths — because this is where R trips people up early.
When you run code interactively, R looks for files starting from your project root (wherever your .Rproj file lives or the root of the folder you opened your with your IDE). Often you will users will find themselves referencing files in various places that are not in the root of their project. Hardcoding out a file path like /home/my-username/folder-that-only-i-have/r-file.R makes this project tied only to that user’s computer. That is not ideal, which is why using paths relative to the project root is so important.
here() from the here package fixes both problems. It detects your project root and always builds paths from there, regardless of how or where the code runs. Use it instead of path() whenever you are building paths to data files.

# here() takes folder names as separate arguments.
# It joins them with the correct separator for your OS.
csv_path <- here("data", "raw", "ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv")

covid_data <- read_csv(csv_path)

title: 5  Visualizing Your Data
text:
5.1 Installing ggplot2
Earlier we filtered Hartford’s data down to a single tidy tibble. You looked at the rows in your console and we moved on. This is great for getting a feel for the data, but it doesn’t necessarily make it easy to get a feel for how the data change over time.
This chapter teaches you how to turn that tibble into a plot that tells the story to someone else — the Commissioner, a journalist, a colleague who doesn’t want to open a CSV.
ggplot2 gives you a grammar — a language for describing what you want the plot to show and it handles the drawing.
Before this chapter can work, install the package once.
install.packages("ggplot2")

# You'll also install extra packages later in this chapter for
# mapping and choropleths.
install.packages(c("tigris", "sf", "mapview"))
Load ggplot2 along with the packages you’ve used so far:
library(ggplot2)

title: 5  Visualizing Your Data
section: 5.2 Building a plot layer by layer
text:
5.2 Building a plot layer by layer

5.2.1 The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 is built on a principle called the Grammar of Graphics. It says every plot is made of layers, each adding something to the picture:








Layer
What it does
Example




Data
The tibble to plot
hartford


Aesthetic mapping
Which columns go on which axis, or to color, size, etc.
x = date, y = new_positives


Geometric object
The shape of the marks
dots, lines, bars, areas


Theme
Non-data ink: fonts, backgrounds, axis styling
removal of grid lines, different fonts



Think of it like making a tiered cake. Data are at the bottom - the biggest layer on which everything is built on top of. Aesthetics are next, and then geometry and finally theme is the the very top. ggplot2 code is more or less written in layers, and it is a helpful mental model that will aid you when you reach for ggplot2 for data story telling.


5.2.2 Your first plot: a scatter plot
We’ll start with the scatter plot.

ggplot(
  data = hartford,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date,
    y = new_positives
  )
) +
  geom_point()








We take our data, our aesthetic and our geometry and we’re already telling stories with those 3 things.
Let’s read them back:

ggplot() starts the plot, supplies the data and the aesthetic mapping (aes) that says “date goes on the x-axis and new_positives goes on the y-axis”.
+ geom_point() adds the layer of dots. The + is what joins layers in ggplot2 — always with a space before and after the +.
Every geometry layer inherits the data and aesthetics from ggplot() unless you override them inside aes() for that specific layer.

The default ggplot2 output works well for internal work, but a briefing needs something cleaner. Let’s build on that first plot.


5.2.3 From dots to a line
Our data is a time-series: date on the x-axis, values on the y-axis. A line makes the trend easier to read.

ggplot(
  data = hartford,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date,
    y = new_positives
  )
) +
  geom_line()








With changing nothing else but the geometry we were able to change the type of plot. This is handy for trying many different kinds of plots with the same data or running different subsets of data through the same geometry to make plots for multiple reports.
This plot still has the default theme’s gray background and the default axis labels read like column names. We’ll work through each of those and make it more presentable.


5.2.4 Title, axis labels, and theme
labs() replaces the automatic labels from column names and adds a title. We use custom CT DPH theme functions to give our plots a clean look — a quick reference lives in the callout below.






NoteCT DPH custom themes



To save time and typing, we will be using CT-DPH specific themes that are saved inside of functions.







Function
What it does




theme_ct_vertical()
Removes the y-axis line and tick marks; use for vertical plots.


theme_ct_horizontal()
Removes the x-axis line and tick marks; use for wide/horizontal plots.


theme_poppins_bold_all()
Sets Poppins, bold face, everywhere in the plot.



And palettes of named CT DPH brand colors:







Function
Colors




list_ct_primary_colors()
primary, primary_shade1 … primary_shade4


list_ct_secondary_colors()
secondary, secondary_shade


list_ct_tertiary_colors()
tertiary, tertiary_shade



These come from the CT DPH brand guide - use the variables, not hex literals, so the branding can change in one place. Further Reading for the full list, code snippets, and tips on plugging colors into ggplot2 scales.



# you can also pipe your data into a plot!

hartford |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(
      x = date,
      y = new_positives
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() + # you can add multiple geometries together
  labs(
    title = "New COVID-19 Cases — Hartford",
    subtitle = "Daily count from report to report (Jun–Jul 2026)",
    x = NULL, # use NULL or an empty string "" to remove the x axis title
    y = "New Cases on Each Date"
  ) +
  theme_ct_vertical()








x = NULL removes the x-axis label entirely — the title is enough, and everyone reading this knows it shows dates.


5.2.5 Adding color
The default plot line uses the first color in the ggplot2 palette. In public health work you probably want a specific color or branding from your organization.
Map the color aesthetic to a string (a color name) to tint both points and line:

ggplot(data = hartford, mapping = aes(x = date, y = new_positives)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3371E7", size = 2, alpha = 0.1) + # alpha sets the transperancy
  geom_line(color = "#3371E7", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "New COVID-19 Cases — Hartford",
    subtitle = "Daily count from report to report (Jun–Jul 2026)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "New Cases on Each Date",
    caption = 'Data as of 2026'
  ) +
  theme_ct_vertical() +
  theme_poppins_bold_all() +
  theme(
    #inside of theme we can interact with specific plot elements and sub-elements
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  )








Two things to notice:

color = "#3371E7" is set outside aes() because it’s a fixed value, not a column. Inside aes(), R would try to map the literal word “#3371E7” to a legend. You rarely want that.
theme_poppins_bold_all() brings the Poppins font everywhere, but we still tweak plot.title and plot.subtitle separately for sizes. Theme layers stack — later ones fill gaps left by earlier ones.

That last plot is the kind of thing you’d paste directly into a briefing slide. You built it piece by piece, and each piece does one thing.


5.2.6 Saving the plot
When you’re happy with a plot, save it to outputs/figures/:

ggsave(
  here("outputs", "figures", "hartford_new_cases.png"),
  width = 7,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 300
)

ggsave() saves the last plot you rendered. No need to name it explicitly — just call it immediately after running the plot.

title: 5  Visualizing Your Data
text:
5.3 Aesthetic mapping
So far you’ve been setting the position of the plot (x and y axis). ggplot2 also maps aesthetics to other properties:








Aesthetic
What it controls
Accepts




x, y
Position on the axes
numeric, date, character


color
Stroke/border color of points and line
column name or fixed color


fill
Fill color of bars, areas
column name or fixed color


size
Size of points or line thickness
column name or fixed size


shape
Point shape (0–24 different shapes)
column name or fixed shape


alpha
Transparency (0 = invisible, 1 = opaque)
column name or fixed value


linetype
Dashed, dotted, etc.
column name or fixed value



When you put a column name inside aes(), ggplot2 creates a legend that tells the reader which values map to which colors, sizes, shapes etc. When you set one outside aes(), the value is fixed and no legend is generated.
To see it in action, add a second line to the same plot — one for total_cases (cumulative) — by mapping y to a column:

#TODO - I don't like this, maybe use deaths or something
ggplot(data = hartford, mapping = aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = new_positives, color = "New Cases"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = total_cases, color = "Cumulative Cases"), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Metric",
    values = c("New Cases" = "#F27124", "Cumulative Cases" = "#3371E7")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "New Cases vs. Cumulative Cases — Hartford",
    y = "Count",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_ct_vertical() +
  theme_poppins_bold_all()

title: 5  Visualizing Your Data
text:
5.4 Choropleth maps
A scatter plot shows change over time. A map shows change across space. For a state-level briefing, the Commissioner might want to see case counts across all the towns at once.
The tigris package fetches official boundary files from the Census Bureau. In our case, we want town boundaries for Connecticut:

library(tigris)
library(sf)

# Fetch CT town boundaries
ct_towns <-
  county_subdivisions(
    state = "09",
    cb = TRUE,
    progress_bar = FALSE
  )

# Show just the outlines on a blank canvas
ct_towns |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "gray95", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_void() # use this for a blank background








Remember our cake analogy? This is our basemap that we will use to layer additional features on top of.
That’s Connecticut’s 169 towns — just outlines. geom_sf() draws spatial data (the sf geometry column). The rest follows the same pattern as every other ggplot2 plot: ggplot() + geom_sf() + labs() + theme().

5.4.1 Coloring towns by case rate
Now join the COVID data to the map by town name and map fill to the case rate:

# Summarize cases by town on the latest date
latest_date <- max(covid_data$`Last update date`, na.rm = TRUE)

town_cases <-
  covid_data |>
  filter(`Last update date` == latest_date) |>
  select(
    Town = Town,
    case_rate = `Case rate`,
    total_cases = `Total cases`
  ) |>
  rename(name = Town)

# Join COVID data to spatial data
ct_bounded <-
  ct_towns |>
  left_join(town_cases, by = join_by(NAME == name))







TipWhat just happened: left_join explained



left_join(x, y, by) keeps every row from the left table (x) and adds matching columns from the right table (y). Where there’s no match, the new columns are filled with NA. Think of it as: “give me all the towns, and bring in any COVID numbers that line up.”
We cover joins in detail in a later chapter — see Further Reading for the full guide.



# Choropleth: gray for towns without data, blue gradient for those with
# TODO: clean up the data
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = ct_bounded[is.na(ct_bounded$case_rate), ],
    fill = "gray95",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = ct_bounded[!is.na(ct_bounded$case_rate), ],
    mapping = aes(fill = case_rate),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#C6D4FB",
    mid = "#7094F5",
    high = "#00214D",
    midpoint = mean(ct_bounded$case_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    na.value = "gray95",
    name = "Case Rate\n(per 100,000)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "COVID-19 Case Rate by Town",
    subtitle = paste("As of", latest_date),
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )








The choropleth tells at a glance which towns carry the heaviest burden. Towns without data (suppressed for small sample sizes) appear gray.






Note



geom_sf() replaces geom_point(), geom_line(), and others when your data is spatial. It reads the geometry column automatically and draws polygons, lines, or points based on the geometry type.








Note



This chapter gave you the foundations of ggplot2 and a taste of spatial visualization. The next chapters add tables (gt), Quarto report-building, functions, and API fetching — the full arc from raw data to self-updating report.

title: 6  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
6.1 The fast way: mapview
The choropleth in the last section is built for a slide — you export it once, drop it into a deck, and it doesn’t change again until the next briefing. That’s exactly what a static ggplot2 map is for.
Not every audience gets a slide, though. A web-facing report, an internal dashboard, or an email to a colleague who wants to click around the map themselves calls for something the reader can zoom, pan, and hover over. That’s an interactive map, and R gives you two ways to build one: mapview for a fast look, and leaflet for a map you build and control piece by piece.
Install both once:
mapview(ct_bounded, zcol = "case_rate")
One line. mapview() looks at ct_bounded, sees it’s spatial data, and automatically:
That’s the trade-off: zero setup, but you don’t control any of it. Use mapview() while you’re exploring a dataset at your desk — checking that a join worked, spotting an outlier town, eyeballing a spatial pattern. When you need a specific popup, a specific color ramp, or a specific basemap for a report someone else will read, reach for leaflet instead.

title: 6  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
picks a basemap and drops your polygons on top of it
colors each town by the case_rate column, since you named it in zcol
builds a legend for that column
wires up hover and click popups showing every attribute column

title: 6  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
6.2 The deliberate way: leaflet
leaflet builds a map the same way ggplot2 builds a plot — one piece at a time. Where ggplot2 chains layers with +, leaflet chains them with the pipe. Read a leaflet chain the same way you read a ggplot2 chain: each step adds one thing to the map.

leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons()





Three steps:

leaflet(ct_bounded) starts the map and supplies the data — like ggplot(data = ...).
addTiles() adds the basemap (streets, place names) from OpenStreetMap.
addPolygons() draws the town boundaries on top of it.

Right now every town is the same flat blue and tells you nothing. Let’s add the pieces one at a time: popups, then color.

6.2.1 Adding popups
A popup is text that appears when someone clicks (or hovers over, with highlightOptions) a polygon. Build the text yourself with paste0(), one string per town, then pass the whole vector to addPolygons():

town_popup <- paste0(
  "<strong>",
  ct_bounded$NAME,
  "</strong><br/>",
  "Case rate: ",
  round(ct_bounded$case_rate, 1),
  " per 100,000<br/>",
  "Total cases: ",
  ct_bounded$total_cases
)

leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(popup = town_popup)





town_popup is a plain character vector, one entry per row of ct_bounded — same length, same order. <strong> and <br/> are HTML tags; leaflet popups render as HTML, so you can bold text and break lines the same way you would on a web page.


6.2.2 Coloring by case rate
colorBin() turns a numeric column into a small palette function — give it bin breaks and colors, and it hands back a function that maps any value in that range to a color. Build the ramp from the CT DPH primary palette so the map matches every other plot in this book:

case_rate_palette <- colorBin(
  palette = c(
    list_ct_primary_colors$primary_shade4,
    list_ct_primary_colors$primary_shade3,
    list_ct_primary_colors$primary,
    list_ct_primary_colors$primary_shade2,
    list_ct_primary_colors$primary_shade1
  ),
  domain = ct_bounded$case_rate,
  bins = 5,
  na.color = "gray95"
)

ct_case_map <-
  leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~ case_rate_palette(case_rate),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = town_popup
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = case_rate_palette,
    values = ~case_rate,
    title = "Case Rate<br/>(per 100,000)",
    position = "bottomright"
  )

ct_case_map





primary_shade4 (the lightest blue) anchors the low end of the ramp, primary_shade1 (the darkest) anchors the high end — light means fewer cases, dark means more, same logic as scale_fill_gradient2() in the static choropleth. ~case_rate_palette(case_rate) uses leaflet’s formula syntax to say “run this function on the case_rate column of the data I gave leaflet() at the start” — it plays the same role aes(fill = case_rate) played earlier.






Tip



Because we built case_rate_palette from list_ct_primary_colors instead of hardcoded hex codes, if the CT DPH brand colors ever change, updating preamble-themes.R updates this map too.

title: 6  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
6.3 Marking a single town
You’ve already met Hartford — the daily new-case line chart earlier in this chapter walked through its case counts day by day. A choropleth shows every town at once, but sometimes you want to point a reader at one town in particular. addMarkers() drops a pin at a specific coordinate on top of the map you already built:

ct_case_map |>
  addMarkers(
    lng = -72.6734,
    lat = 41.7658,
    popup = "Hartford — click here to see the daily new-case trend for this town."
  )





Piping addMarkers() onto ct_case_map adds the pin without rebuilding the choropleth underneath it — the same “keep adding layers” habit you’ve been using since the first ggplot2 scatter plot.

title: 6  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
6.4 Saving and exporting
An interactive map only stays interactive where something can run JavaScript — a rendered HTML report, a Shiny app, a browser. Paste it into a Word document or a PDF and it becomes a flat image anyway, so mapview::mapshot() lets you export either format depending on where the map is going.
Save the fully interactive version as its own HTML file — useful when you want to embed it in a Quarto HTML report with an <iframe>, or email it to someone who can open it and click around themselves:

mapshot(
  ct_case_map,
  url = here(
    "chapters",
    "03-data-visualization",
    "maps",
    "ct-case-rate-map.html"
  )
)

Save a static snapshot as PNG when the destination can’t run JavaScript at all — a slide deck, a printed briefing, a PDF report:

mapshot(
  ct_case_map,
  file = here(
    "chapters",
    "03-data-visualization",
    "maps",
    "ct-case-rate-map.png"
  )
)

Rule of thumb: if the report renders to HTML and the reader is looking at a screen, keep the map interactive. If it renders to PDF, Word, or a printed page, export a PNG instead.






Note



This section covered enough leaflet to build a colored, clickable choropleth. leaflet can also layer multiple datasets, add custom basemaps, cluster hundreds of markers, and respond to clicks with Shiny — Further Reading has a deeper dive into leaflet waiting for when you need it.

title: 7  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
7.1 What is an API!?
To put it simply, An API1 or application programming interface can be thought of in part as another tool in the user’s tool belt to programmatically interact and often extract data without having to manually download data. No one needs to lift their mouse and search through a webpage and click download. This is a simple, yet powerful concept that extend to many areas of data work and beyond. I encourage users to read up on and develop their API skills beyond what is presented in our coursework.

title: 7  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
7.2 Working with httr2
We will be working with httr2 as our package of choice for API work. Often, specific APIs will have their own packages for working with them, it is often better to use those, but we cannot cover them all, and not every API has its own package. httr2 will always be here for us, and if users can understand httr2 then picking up the other more specific packages will become even easier.
Remember our Covid-19 pandemic dataset? Before we would navigate to that website and download the datafile, or perhaps rely on the snippet of data provided in this course. No more - we are far too busy for that kind of work. From here on out we will be using the API, and in the future when users encounter data they want to incorporate into their analyses - it is almost always better to use the API.
Install httr2 like we would any other package.

install.packages('httr2')

Next we’ll attach the httr2 and dplyr packages to our session.

library(dplyr) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages() # this silences dplyr messages when loading the package
library(httr2)


7.2.1 httr2 requests and responses
Recall our pandemic data’s landing page - notice what pops up when you click the ‘Export’ button in the top right of the webpage. The popup has ‘Download file’ defaulting to ‘Export format’ of csv. However, right next to it is ‘API endpoint’ - click that and notice the ‘Data format’ switches to ‘JSON’. Below that you may notice that there is a ‘Version’ toggle for either ‘SODA3’ or ‘SODA2’. For now, select ‘SODA2’ and copy the url provided, it should look like this: https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json now that we have our url or endpoint as they are often called let’s hop into the code.

# save our url into an object so we don't have to type it out everywhere
endpoint <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json"

# We build our data request up piece by piece

my_request <- request(endpoint) # base of the request

# Get a our response from the Open Data Portal API

odp_response <-
  my_request |>
  req_perform() # perform the request, and get a response base

odp_response

<httr2_response>
GET https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json
Status: 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Body: In memory (412447 bytes)




7.2.2 Extracting data from responses
We have a response - now where is our data? We need to pull it out of the body of the response and then convert it into an R dataframe.

my_odp_data <-
  odp_response |>
  resp_body_json() |> # extract the data, it's returned as an R list
  bind_rows() # for this endpoint we can easily convert to a dataframe

my_odp_data

Lovely - but how come there are only 1000 rows? That leads us to our next wrinkle when working with APIs. This one is public, so just about anyone can hammer on this API at anytime, and some of data can be quite large. In order to prevent users from accidentally running a massive query for data they may not even need (and to prevent misuse from unscrupulous types) APIs will often only send a small chunk of the data and then offer up ways to retrieve the next chunk, and then the next chunk, and so on and so forth. This can be accomplished in a few different ways, but for this API they use pages with limits and offsets.






Note



Users working with different APIs should read that API’s documentation to see how that specific API handles pagination/iteration through responses.

title: 7  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
7.3 Extracting all data
We’re going to have to do a little leg work here to get all the data, and then I am going to show you how you can package this all up so you can reuse it over and over again.
First, users need to understand what the limit and offset are and how they can leverage those to get the data they expect.

limit: The total number of rows of data brought back in the request.

The default for this API and this endpoint is 1000. Some datasets might be small like 5000 rows. You can just bump this number up to 5000 and pull it all in one go.

offset: The starting point row number for the query.

The default for this API is 0, because it starts at the first row.


These two parameters can be used in conjunction to, for example, grab the first 1000 rows of a dataset, and then grab the next 1000 and so on and so forth until all data is had.

7.3.1 Modifying the limit and offset
So modifying the limit and offset is all well in good, but how do we actually go about changing those values? Remember our endpoint url? Thankfully these are parameters that can be tacked on to the end of the url.
If for whatever reason we wanted the 10th row, and only the 10th row of our dataset we can modify our url to look like this:
https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json?$limit=1&$offset=9
Notice that the parameters come at the end of the original url after a ?. Users then append $limit= and & and $offset= with the desired values. Feel free to try this in your web browser - most modern browsers will display the data from the response.






Note



Note that items/data are zero-indexed, meaning the first item the data is ‘row’ 0. To grab the 10th item we skip the first 9 items.


Do not take my word for it. Try this out: click on https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json?$limit=10&$offset=0 and make note of the tenth item.
It should look something like this:
{
    "lastupdatedate":"2022-06-24T00:00:00.000",
    "town_no":"10","town":"Bethlehem",
    "towntotalcases":"620",
    "townconfirmedcases":"529",
    "townprobablecases":"91",
    "towncaserate":"18225",
    "towntotaldeaths":"3",
    "townconfirmeddeaths":"2",
    "townprobabledeaths":"1",
    "peopletested":"2781",
    "ratetested100k":"81746",
    "numberoftests":"11841",
    "numberofpositives":"749",
    "numberofnegatives":"11070",
    "numberofindeterminates":"22"
}
Does that match our original single item we had before?


7.3.2 Using httr2
No one wants to modify urls by hand, and we’re still clicking through everything, time to use httr2 to do the heavy lifting.

# We're going to grab first 5000 rows, 1000 rows at a time.
# so we will query 1000 rows, 5 times

req <-
  request(endpoint) |>
  # don't forget the $ as part of the parameter name for this api
  # backticks are required for nonstandard r names
  req_url_query(
    `$limit` = 1000,
    `$offset` = 0
  )


resps <-
  req_perform_iterative(
    req,
    next_req = iterate_with_offset(
      param_name = "$offset",
      start = 0,
      offset = 1000
    ),
    max_reqs = 5
  )

# resps contains a list of 5 responses
# we want to take each response and do what we did above to all of them
# we will use an anonymous function otherwise known as lambda functions in
# other programming languages

data <-
  resps |>
  resps_data(
    \(resp) {
      # declare the name of each item in our resps list
      resp |> # for each response in our responses
        resp_body_json() |> # convert the json to a list
        bind_rows() # bind these into a dataframe
    }
  )

 4 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 4       Avon        3030           2773              
 5 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 5       Barkhamsted 527            490               
 6 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 6       Beacon Fal… 1306           1163              
 7 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 7       Berlin      4098           3751              
 8 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 8       Bethany     991            901

10 2022-06-24T00:00:00.000 10      Bethlehem   620            529               
# ℹ 4,990 more rows
# ℹ 11 more variables: townprobablecases <chr>, towncaserate <chr>,
#   towntotaldeaths <chr>, townconfirmeddeaths <chr>, townprobabledeaths <chr>,
#   peopletested <chr>, ratetested100k <chr>, numberoftests <chr>,
#   numberofpositives <chr>, numberofnegatives <chr>,
#   numberofindeterminates <chr>




7.3.3 All the data everywhere, all at once
Wait - weren’t we promised all the data!? Fair point, how do we grab that data if we don’t know how many rows there are? At time of writing there are 102245 rows in this dataset, but let’s pretend we do not know that, and often that is the case.

# bump this up to 10k rows per request and 10k offset each times
number_of_rows <- 10000

# first request grabs the first 10k
req <-
  request(endpoint) |>
  req_url_query(
    `$limit` = number_of_rows,
    `$offset` = 0
  )

# drop the max_reqs argument
resps <-
  req_perform_iterative(
    req,
    progress = FALSE, # the progress bar is super cool, but doesn't play nicely with the website, feel free to leave it on!
    next_req = iterate_with_offset(
      param_name = "$offset",
      start = 0,
      offset = number_of_rows
    )
  )

data <-
  resps |>
  resps_data(
    \(resp) {
      resp |>
        resp_body_json() |>
        bind_rows()
    }
  )

nrow(data) == 102245

[1] TRUE


Look at that! We have our 102245 rows.






Warning



Start small when working with a new endpoint
Users will often want all the data, but they will often not know how many rows there are. Use caution when grabbing everything, there may be more data than can be handled at once.

title: 7  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
7.4 Functions crash course
By now users may have noticed that we’ve written the same or similar chain of request and response a few times now. Let us tidy this up into something we can reuse over and over - a function! The httr2 documentation has a wonderful section on wrapping apis into useful functions that I will encourage users to read.
We will take much of the logic and code discussed in that document and apply it to our usecases.
Up to this point users will be using functions all over the place in R. Now we are going to write out own using the function() function to encapsulate our logic. We will do this time and time again. We create our function by providing the inputs it expects, and then perform the actions we want it to do with those inputs. Good functions typically will do one thing or step really well, and have a descriptive name. It is usually good to create and chain a few smaller functions instead of having one massive function.
Let’s start by creating a function that reduces the amount of repetitive typing we need to do, smooths over some API rough edges and finally returns all the data.
Take one more look at our endpoint: https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json. Notice anything? If we’re always using the Open Data Portal, the domain (data.ct.gov) is always going to be the same. There is always going to be a ‘/resource/’ section and always a ‘.json’. The only real part that is going to change is the resource id (often called a four by four on this portal). So that is probably a good target for input from users.

# our function will be called fetch all data
fetch_all_data <-
  function(resource, rows = 10000) {
    # Fetch all data from the provided resource id for the CT Open Data Portal
    #
    # resource: string - Required portal "four by four" in the format 'xxxx-xxxx'
    # rows: numeric - Number of rows of data to fetch one response at a time.
    #   defaults to 100000 and becomes the LIMIT and OFFSET for the request.
    # Returns: A tibble

    # handle the resource from the user

    base <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource"

    # create the first request
    req <-
      request(base) |>
      req_url_path_append(resource) |> #appened the user provided 4x4 to the base url
      req_url_query(
        `$limit` = rows, # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        `$offset` = 0 # start with the first row
      )

    # perform the request and then with each request increment the offset by `rows`
    resps <-
      req_perform_iterative(
        req,
        progress = FALSE,
        next_req = iterate_with_offset(
          param_name = "$offset",
          start = 0,
          offset = rows # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        )
      )

    # convert the response objects from the API to a tibble of data
    # for each response from the API grab the json body, convert to an R list
    # and then squash all that into a singular tibble
    data <-
      resps |>
      resps_data(
        \(resp) {
          resp |>
            resp_body_json() |>
            bind_rows()
        }
      )

    return(data)
  }

We wrote our function, now let us take it for a spin. Our resource ID was 28fr-iqnx.

# === setup ===
library(dplyr)
library(httr2)
library(lubridate)

# === constants ===
RESOURCE <- "28fr-iqnx"

# === functions ===
fetch_all_data <-
  function(resource, rows = 10000) {
    # Fetch all data from the provided resource id for the CT Open Data Portal
    #
    # resource: string - Required portal "four by four" in the format 'xxxx-xxxx'
    # rows: numeric - Number of rows of data to fetch one response at a time.
    #   defaults to 100000 and becomes the LIMIT and OFFSET for the request.
    # Returns: A tibble

    # handle the resource from the user

    base <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource"

    # create the first request
    req <-
      request(base) |>
      req_url_path_append(resource) |> #append the user provided 4x4 to the base url
      req_url_query(
        `$limit` = rows, # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        `$offset` = 0 # start with the first row
      )

    # perform the request and then with each request increment the offset by `rows`
    resps <-
      req_perform_iterative(
        req,
        progress = FALSE,
        next_req = iterate_with_offset(
          param_name = "$offset",
          start = 0,
          offset = rows # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        )
      )

    # convert the response objects from the API to a tibble of data
    # for each response from the API grab the json body, convert to an R list
    # and then squash all that into a singular tibble
    data <-
      resps |>
      resps_data(
        \(resp) {
          resp |>
            resp_body_json() |>
            bind_rows()
        }
      )

    return(data)
  }

# === main ===
main <- function() {
  # main entrypoint into our analysis

  # data ingestion
  data <- fetch_all_data(resource = RESOURCE)

  # key measures
  total_tests <-
    data |>
    mutate(date = ymd_hms(lastupdatedate)) |>
    filter(date == max(date)) |>
    reframe(
      total_pandemic_tests = sum(
        as.numeric(numberoftests),
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
    ) |>
    pull(total_pandemic_tests)

  cat(
    paste(
      "The total number of pandemic tests in these data were:",
      format(total_tests, big.mark = ',')
    )
  )
}

# === entrypoint ===
main()

The total number of pandemic tests in these data were: 16,515,446

12.3 Custom themes and color palettes
The book ships three ggplot2 theme helpers and several named color palettes in preamble-themes.R. Each chapter sources this file at the top so the functions are available throughout.

12.3.1 Theme functions








Function
What it does
Use when…




theme_ct_vertical()
Removes the y-axis line, y-axis tick marks and x-axis tick marks. Sets axis titles to bold Poppins.
Vertical / tall plots (time series, vertical bars)


theme_ct_horizontal()
Removes the x-axis line, x-axis tick marks and y-axis tick marks. Sets axis titles to bold Poppins.
Horizontal / wide plots (horizontal bars, side-by-side comparisons)


theme_poppins_bold_all()
Sets every bit of text in the plot to bold Poppins.
When you want a uniform, no-nonsense look across all elements



Theme functions stack — call them with + like any other ggplot2 layer. Later themes fill gaps left by earlier ones, so the ordering matters only when they overlap.


12.3.2 Color palettes







Function
Colors returned




list_ct_primary_colors()
primary (#3371E7), primary_shade1 (#00214D), primary_shade2 (#003D9C), primary_shade3 (#7094F5), primary_shade4 (#C6D4FB)


list_ct_secondary_colors()
secondary (#F27124), secondary_shade (#FAAA19)


list_ct_tertiary_colors()
tertiary (#D8343E), tertiary_shade (#94343E)


list_old_sha_colors()
Legacy SHA palette — use only for backward-compat with older reports


list_color_hex_codes()
Nested list of all palettes above (flat list of named hex values)



Always use the variables, not hex literals. If the brand updates its palette, a single change to preamble-themes.R propagates to every plot.
To pick one or two named colors inside a scale, slice the returned list:

library(ggplot2)
source(file.path(here::here(), "preamble-themes.R"))

ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(x = factor(1:2), y = c(15, 25),
               fill = factor(c("New Cases", "New Cases"))),
           position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = list_ct_primary_colors[c("primary_shade1", "primary_shade3")]
  ) +
  theme_poppins_bold_all() +
  theme_ct_vertical()

title: 13  Joins
text:
13.1 left_join(): keep everything on the left
The choropleth section used left_join() to attach COVID case data to town boundaries. That’s one of six join verbs dplyr gives you — each answers a different question about how two tables relate. This page walks through all six using the same shape of data: a towns table (the “left” table, like ct_towns) and a cases table (the “right” table, like town_cases).
towns has four rows, cases has three, and only two names (Hartford, New Haven) appear in both. Norwalk has no case data. Stamford has case data but isn’t in towns. That mismatch is exactly what makes joins interesting — each verb handles it differently.
towns |>
  left_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  name       county    case_rate
  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford   Hartford        412
2 New Haven  New Haven       388
3 Bridgeport Fairfield        NA
4 Norwalk    Fairfield        NA
Every row from towns survives. Where cases has no matching name (Norwalk), case_rate comes back NA. Stamford never appears — it wasn’t in the left table to begin with. This is what the choropleth uses: keep all 169 CT towns, fill in case data where it exists, show gray for the rest.

title: 13  Joins
section: 13.2 right_join(): keep everything on the right
text:
13.2 right_join(): keep everything on the right

towns |>
  right_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name      county    case_rate
  <chr>     <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford  Hartford        412
2 New Haven New Haven       388
3 Stamford  <NA>            355


The mirror image. Every row from cases survives, including Stamford, which now shows NA for county. Norwalk drops out entirely since it’s not in cases. In practice, right_join(x, y) is the same as left_join(y, x) with the columns reordered — most people just pick whichever table they name first and use left_join().

title: 13  Joins
text:
13.3 inner_join(): keep only matches

towns |>
  inner_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  name      county    case_rate
  <chr>     <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford  Hartford        412
2 New Haven New Haven       388


Only rows present in both tables survive: Hartford and New Haven. No NAs, because everything left in the result has a match on both sides. Use this when a row without a match is meaningless for what you’re calculating — e.g., a rate that requires both a population and a case count.

title: 13  Joins
text:
13.4 full_join(): keep everything from both

towns |>
  full_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  name       county    case_rate
  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford   Hartford        412
2 New Haven  New Haven       388
3 Bridgeport Fairfield        NA
4 Norwalk    Fairfield        NA
5 Stamford   <NA>            355


Nothing is dropped. Norwalk keeps its row with case_rate as NA; Stamford keeps its row with county as NA. Use this when you want a complete picture of every name that shows up anywhere, gaps and all.

title: 13  Joins
text:
13.5 semi_join(): filter, don’t add columns

towns |>
  semi_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  name      county   
  <chr>     <chr>    
1 Hartford  Hartford 
2 New Haven New Haven


semi_join() keeps rows from towns that have a match in cases — but it never adds cases’ columns. The result has only name and county. Think of it as a filter, not a join: “give me the towns that also appear in my case data.”

title: 13  Joins
text:
13.6 anti_join(): the opposite filter

towns |>
  anti_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  name       county   
  <chr>      <chr>    
1 Bridgeport Fairfield
2 Norwalk    Fairfield


The inverse of semi_join(): keep rows from towns that have no match in cases. This is the fastest way to answer “which towns are missing case data?” — exactly the gray towns in the choropleth.






TipPicking the right join




Need every row from your main table, filled in where possible? → left_join()
Need only rows that exist on both sides? → inner_join()
Need every row from either side, gaps and all? → full_join()
Just need to filter one table by presence in another, without adding columns? → semi_join() / anti_join()

title: 14  Working with Excel Files
text:
14.2 Reading .xlsx files
readxl reads Excel files the same way readr reads CSVs. Use here() to build the path so it works both interactively and during render.

library(readxl)
library(here)

xlsx_path <- here("data", "raw", "your-file.xlsx")
your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path)

your_data

If your workbook has multiple sheets, use the sheet argument:

your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet = "Sheet2")

# or by position
your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet = 2)

title: 14  Working with Excel Files
text:
14.3 Writing .xlsx files
writexl writes a data frame to an Excel file with no Java dependency (unlike openxlsx).

library(writexl)
library(here)

output_path <- here("data", "my-output.xlsx")

write_xlsx(your_data, path = output_path)

To write multiple sheets in one workbook, pass a named list:

write_xlsx(
  list(
    cases  = cases_data,
    deaths = deaths_data
  ),
  path = output_path
)

14.4 When to use CSV vs Excel
Prefer CSV for anything that feeds into analysis — it is plain text, version-control friendly, and readable by every tool. Use Excel output when the end recipient is a stakeholder who will open the file directly in Excel and expects formatting.

text:
15.1 CSV
Once you have cleaned or summarized data, you will want to write it back out. This chapter covers the most common output formats.
write_csv() from readr is the default for analysis outputs that feed into other scripts or tools.
library(readr)
library(here)

output_path <- here("data", "processed", "ct_covid_clean.csv")

write_csv(your_data, file = output_path)

title: 15  Writing Data Files
section: 15.2 Checking and cleaning up with fs
text:
15.2 Checking and cleaning up with fs
fs lets you inspect and manage files from inside R — useful for verifying that a write succeeded or cleaning up intermediate files.

library(fs)
library(here)

# list everything in a folder
dir_ls(path = here("data", "processed"))

# check whether specific files exist
files <- dir_ls(path = here("data"), glob = "*my-new-file*")
file_exists(files)

# delete files
file_delete(files)
file_exists(files)

title: 15  Writing Data Files
text:
15.3 Parquet
Parquet is a compressed columnar format that reads and writes much faster than CSV for large datasets. It is a better default than CSV once your data exceeds a few hundred thousand rows.

install.packages("arrow")


library(arrow)
library(here)

output_path <- here("data", "processed", "ct_covid_clean.parquet")

write_parquet(your_data, sink = output_path)

# reading it back
your_data <- read_parquet(output_path)

Parquet files are not human-readable in a text editor, but they are interoperable — Python, Spark, DuckDB, and most modern data tools can read the same file.
